itens.resumo: A heresy that attributed to Christ a single will, the divine one, in an attempt at reconciliation with the Monophysites that compromised the integrity of his human nature.
itens.corpo:
In the early seventh century, the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, faced with the need to restore the religious unity of an empire weakened by wars against the Persians and, soon afterward, by the Arab-Muslim expansion, sponsored a political and theological effort to reconcile the Eastern Monophysites, who were the majority in strategic regions such as Egypt and Syria, with the faith of Chalcedon. Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople formulated for this purpose a compromise formula: although Christ did in fact possess two natures, divine and human, as Chalcedon had defined, in him there would be only one energy or operation (Monoenergism) and, in a later refinement of the same idea, only one will (from the Greek "monos", single, and "thelema", will), which is Monotheletism proper, resulting from the perfect identification between the human will and the divine will of Christ. In 634, Sergius even obtained the formal adherence of a synod gathered in Cyprus to his formula.

Seeking support from the West as well, Sergius wrote to Pope Honorius I, who replied in ambiguous terms, speaking of "one will" in Christ. This letter would be used decades later as proof that a pope had come to subscribe, though perhaps without full awareness of the technical implications, to a formula that would prove to be heretical. Historians still debate whether Honorius truly intended to endorse Monotheletism or merely to avoid verbal controversies, but the episode would become a required case study in later debates on the limits of papal infallibility. The main theological opponent of Monotheletism was the monk Maximus the Confessor, who argued with great rigor that denying Christ a distinct human will, even one perfectly submissive to the divine will, amounted to denying him a complete and free humanity. Because of his resistance, Maximus was imprisoned, had his tongue and right hand mutilated by imperial order, and died in 662, in exile, shortly after these torments.

The Third Council of Constantinople, the sixth ecumenical council, held between 680 and 681, formally rejected Monotheletism and Monoenergism as heresies, defining that Christ possesses two natural and distinct wills and two natural operations, corresponding to his two natures, united without division or conflict, with the human will freely and actively submitted to the divine will, without being absorbed, annulled or diminished in its integrity by it. The council condemned by name the main defenders and promoters of the doctrine, among them the patriarchs Sergius, Pyrrhus and Paul of Constantinople, and also, notably and with no precedent in conciliar history, the already deceased Pope Honorius I, whose condemnation by an ecumenical council would later be confirmed by successive popes throughout the Middle Ages, becoming one of the episodes most discussed by theologians and historians of the Church when dealing with the limits of the papal magisterium.
itens.condenacao: Third Council of Constantinople (680-681)

itens.resumo: An eighth-century Hispanic heresy according to which Christ would be Son of God by nature only in his divinity, being "adopted" as son in his humanity.
itens.corpo:
After the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula in 711, the ancient Hispano-Visigothic Church survived as a tolerated Christian minority — the Mozarabic community — under the rule of the emirs of Córdoba. It was in this environment that Elipandus, Archbishop of Toledo since the middle of the eighth century and the highest ecclesiastical authority of Islamic Hispania, formulated — or, according to another historiographical reading, merely took up and systematized an old Hispanic Christological formula of Isidorian flavor — the doctrine that would come to be known as Adoptionism: Christ would be Son of God "by nature" only as the eternal Word, consubstantial with the Father, but "by adoption," an "adoptive" or "nuncupative" son, as man, in his concrete humanity born of Mary. The controversy took shape from the middle of the 780s, when Elipandus was already coming from an earlier dispute, about the Trinity, with a Sevillian monk named Migetius; the adoptive formula then seemed to him a way of clearly reaffirming the full humanity of Christ against the errors of Migetius, without realizing — according to his adversaries — that it dangerously divided the one person of the Son into two "sons," one by nature and the other by adoption.

Felix, Bishop of Urgell, on the frontier between the Carolingian Spanish March and the Muslim territories, adhered to and gave theological sophistication to the same doctrine, becoming, in the eyes of his Frankish adversaries, the principal intellectual author of the heresy — to the point that it was also called the "Felician heresy." The thesis met with immediate opposition in free Christian Hispania: the monk Beatus of Liébana, of the Asturian monastery of San Martín de Turieno (today Santo Toribio de Liébana), already famous for his monumental "Commentary on the Apocalypse" — a work that would become the model for the famous illuminated codices known as "Beatus manuscripts" — and Bishop Etherius of Osma wrote, around 785, a joint treatise against Elipandus, accusing him in harsh terms of madness, ignorance, and even of being a "testicle of the Antichrist." Informed of the dispute, Pope Adrian I sent a letter that same year condemning the adoptive doctrine as a re-edition, in new garb, of the ancient Nestorianism.

The center of the conflict shifted, however, to the court of Charlemagne, to whom Felix of Urgell was subject as a Frankish subject. Summoned to explain himself at the Council of Regensburg in 792, Felix abjured the doctrine before papal legates — but, back in his diocese, he retracted his own retraction and returned to professing Adoptionism, claiming to have made it under duress. Alcuin of York, Charlemagne's most influential theological adviser, then devoted himself to systematically refuting the heresy in successive works — a "Libellus adversus Felicis haeresim" and later the "Seven Books against Felix of Urgell" — and exchanged letters, more conciliatory in tone but equally firm, with Elipandus himself.

The case was judged at the Council of Frankfurt, convened by Charlemagne in 794 and gathered with the participation of legates of Pope Adrian I and of bishops from all of Francia, Italy, and England. The assembly solemnly condemned Adoptionism, reaffirming that Christ is the only Son of God, truly so by nature both in his divinity and in his humanity, without any adoptive sense. Felix, pressed once more, appeared at Aachen, heard the refutation of several bishops, and abjured again; he was then kept under watchful custody in Lyon, where Archbishop Leidrad and, after him, Agobard of Lyon continued to follow him closely, and where he ended his days without it being known for certain whether he maintained a sincere retraction to the end.

Elipandus, protected by distance and by the relative autonomy of the Mozarabic Church under Islamic rule, where Charlemagne's authority did not reach, never retracted and died still Archbishop of Toledo, around the beginning of the ninth century, maintaining the adoptive formula to the end. Hispanic Adoptionism, understood by some historians also as an attempt — even if involuntary — to make Christian Christology more palatable to the strict monotheism of Islam then dominant in the Peninsula, did not survive as an organized movement after the death of its two principal defenders, but remained for centuries an obligatory reference in the manuals of heresiology, alongside Nestorianism, of which it was seen as a medieval reincarnation.
itens.condenacao: Council of Frankfurt (794)

itens.resumo: A movement that rejected the veneration of sacred images as idolatry, going so far as to promote the systematic destruction of icons in the Byzantine Empire.
itens.corpo:
The iconoclast crisis was born in the Byzantine Empire under Emperor Leo III the Isaurian (r. 717-741), founder of a new dynasty who had come to the throne shortly after repelling an Arab siege of Constantinople. Convinced that the veneration of icons had degenerated into idolatry — and perhaps influenced by Muslim and Jewish criticism of religious images, besides interpreting military defeats and a volcanic eruption in the Aegean Sea as signs of divine displeasure — Leo III promoted, from around 726-730, the removal of sacred images from public places, beginning with the famous icon of Christ above the Bronze Gate of the imperial palace. Patriarch Germanus I of Constantinople, who refused to subscribe to the new policy, was forced to resign in 730.

The most influential theological defense of the veneration of images came, paradoxically, from beyond the direct reach of imperial power: the monk Saint John of Damascus, who lived under Muslim rule in the monastery of Mar Saba, near Jerusalem, wrote three «Apologetic Discourses against Those Who Decry the Holy Images», in which he distinguished precisely between «latria» (adoration), owed to God alone, and «proskynesis» or relative veneration, given to the image by reason of the one it represents — arguing further that, since God himself had made himself visible in the Incarnation of Christ, it had become legitimate to represent the incarnate Son visually and, by extension, the saints who reflect him.

Under Constantine V (r. 741-775), son of Leo III, the iconoclast policy became more radical and gained conciliar justification: in 754, a council gathered at Hieria, with the participation of 338 bishops but none of the five patriarchates — not even that of Constantinople, then vacant —, declared the veneration of images a form of idolatry and anathematized by name its main defenders, including John of Damascus. Decades of systematic persecution followed: icons and mosaics were destroyed or covered with whitewash in churches throughout the empire, and many monks — traditionally the most fervent defenders of images — were imprisoned, tortured, exiled or killed, while entire monasteries were closed or converted to civil uses.

The turnaround came with the death of Leo IV and the regency of Constantine VI's mother, Empress Irene, who in 787 convened the Second Council of Nicaea — recognized as the seventh ecumenical council — gathering about 350 bishops. The council condemned iconoclasm, solemnly restored the veneration of images, and established the distinction, already sketched by John of Damascus, between the relative honor due to icons and the adoration reserved to God alone. In the West, however, a deficient Latin translation of the acts of the council led Charlemagne and his theologians to believe, mistakenly, that Nicaea II required adoration of images; the reaction to this misunderstanding resulted in the «Libri Carolini» and was discussed again, in passing, at the Council of Frankfurt in 794 (see the entry on Adoptionism).

The controversy was not, however, over: under Leo V the Armenian, from 815, a new council gathered in Hagia Sophia reaffirmed iconoclasm, inaugurating a second phase of persecution that struck hard at figures such as Abbot Theodore the Studite, a leading exponent of monastic resistance. Only with the death of Emperor Theophilos in 842, and the regency of his widow, Empress Theodora, in the name of her minor son Michael III, was the question resolved definitively: in 843, a synod convened with the new Patriarch Methodios irrevocably restored the veneration of images, in an episode celebrated liturgically every year, on the first Sunday of Lent, as the «Triumph of Orthodoxy» — a feast that the Eastern Orthodox Churches keep to this day.
itens.condenacao: Second Council of Nicaea (787); reaffirmed in the "Triumph of Orthodoxy" (843)

itens.resumo: Rupture between Pope Nicholas I and Patriarch Photius of Constantinople, involving disputes over jurisdiction and the Filioque, and considered a direct forerunner of the East-West Schism of 1054.
itens.corpo:
Photius, a layman of vast erudition who held high offices in the Byzantine imperial administration, was the author of the «Bibliotheca» (or «Myriobiblon»), a compendium of summaries and critical commentaries on hundreds of works of Greek, pagan and Christian antiquity, many of them now lost and known only through his testimony — an achievement that would make him, regardless of the controversy that would give him lasting fame, one of the most important intellectual figures of the Byzantine cultural renaissance of the ninth century. In 858, Emperor Michael III and his uncle and de facto regent, the Caesar Bardas, deposed Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, who was in conflict with the court, and raised Photius to the patriarchate in a very rapid succession of orders — within a few days, the then layman became a monk, deacon, priest and bishop —, a canonically irregular procedure that was already enough to fuel strong opposition among Ignatius's partisans.

Pope Nicholas I, informed of the deposition of Ignatius and of the hurried ordination of Photius, sent legates to Constantinople to investigate the case; upon finding, in his view, irregularities in the process, Nicholas gathered a synod in Rome in 863, which declared Photius's elevation null and reaffirmed Ignatius as the legitimate patriarch — a decision interpreted in Constantinople as an unacceptable interference by the Bishop of Rome in the internal affairs of a sister Church, aggravating already long-standing tensions over jurisdiction.

The dispute took on a doctrinal dimension when it was joined to the question of newly converted Bulgaria: the Bulgarian khan Boris I, baptized in 864 with a Byzantine godfather, dissatisfied with the degree of ecclesiastical autonomy that Constantinople offered him, turned in 866 to Rome and to the Frankish missionaries of Emperor Louis the German — missionaries who brought to Bulgaria, among other Latin practices foreign to Byzantine usage, the «Filioque» clause, already current in the Frankish West. Photius reacted in 867 with an encyclical addressed to the other Eastern patriarchs, denouncing the Filioque as an illegitimate addition to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed and calling it the «crown of evils» brought by the Frankish missionaries, and he convoked a council in Constantinople which, in a symmetrical response to Rome, declared Pope Nicholas I himself deposed and excommunicated.

The political turn of events ended the impasse faster than theology did: in September 867, Michael III was assassinated in a palace coup by his former colleague Basil, who became emperor as Basil I and, seeking legitimacy and reconciliation with both Rome and the partisans of Ignatius, deposed Photius and restored Ignatius to the patriarchate. Nicholas I had died a few months earlier, in November of the same year, without seeing the outcome. A council held in Constantinople between 869 and 870 — recognized by the Catholic Church as the eighth ecumenical council, but rejected as such by Orthodoxy — formally condemned Photius.

The story had, however, a more ambiguous ending than a simple definitive condemnation: with the death of Ignatius in 877, Basil I himself restored Photius to the patriarchate, and a new council in Constantinople, between 879 and 880, reaffirmed his position with the apparent acquiescence of papal legates — a council that the Orthodox Church considers, for its part, the true eighth ecumenical council, although it never definitively resolved the question of the Filioque or of jurisdiction over Bulgaria. Photius would be deposed a second and final time in 886 by Emperor Leo VI, dying around 893; the Orthodox Church has venerated him ever since as Saint Photius the Great.

More than a formal and definitive schism — communion between Rome and Constantinople was restored, albeit unstably, after 867 —, the Photian episode exposed in advance exactly the same fault lines that, almost two centuries later, would become irreversible in the East-West Schism of 1054: the legitimacy of the Filioque clause, the limits of papal jurisdiction over Eastern churches, and the contest over spheres of missionary influence in the Balkans. For this reason, Church historians usually treat the Photian Schism as a dress rehearsal, or direct forerunner, of the definitive rupture of 1054.
itens.condenacao: Mutual excommunications between Rome and Constantinople (863-867), with partial reconciliation after the death of Nicholas I

itens.resumo: Spiritual doctrine of Father Miguel de Molinos that preached the total annihilation of one's own will and passive abandonment to God as the path to Christian perfection.
itens.corpo:
Miguel de Molinos was born in 1628 in Muniesa, in the Aragonese region of Teruel, and studied theology at the Jesuit college of Saint Paul in Valencia before being ordained a priest in 1652. He moved to Rome in the mid-1660s, where he quickly gained exceptional fame as a confessor and spiritual director, attracting penitents among the nobility, the clergy and even cardinals — among them Benedetto Odescalchi, who would be elected pope in 1676 with the name Innocent XI and who, for years, counted among his protectors.

His principal work, the «Spiritual Guide», published in Rome in 1675 with favorable ecclesiastical approbations, proposed a path of interior prayer centered on recollection, silence and the total passive abandonment of the soul to God — a state of «quiet» in which the active faculties of reasoning, imagining and even willing were to be suspended, letting God act directly in the soul without discursive effort on the part of the one praying. The book was enormously successful: it reached twenty editions in twelve years and was translated into Latin, French, English and German, becoming one of the most widely circulated prayer manuals of seventeenth-century Catholic Europe.

Criticism, however, grew rapidly, above all from the Jesuits, Molinos's rivals in the spiritual direction of the Roman elite, who saw in his doctrine of quiet a risk of moral indifference: if the soul passively united to God should no longer exercise active resistance of the will, the critics argued, a dangerous opening would be created to justify moral lapses as something foreign to the true «self» already surrendered to God — an accusation reinforced by rumors, raised during the trial, of improper conduct by Molinos with penitents. To these factors was added a political component: King Louis XIV of France, at odds with Pope Innocent XI for other reasons of ecclesiastical policy, pressed Rome against a spiritual movement that had the support of cardinals close to the pope.

Arrested by the Holy Office in May 1685, Molinos was tried over the course of two years; on 3 September 1687, before a great crowd in the Dominican church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, he was declared a dogmatic heretic and obliged to abjure publicly. Shortly afterward, Pope Innocent XI promulgated the apostolic constitution «Coelestis Pastor» (1687), condemning as heretical, suspect, erroneous or scandalous sixty-eight propositions drawn from his writings and from his trial. Molinos was sentenced to life imprisonment and to continuous public penance, dying incarcerated in Rome in December 1696, never having regained his freedom.

Attenuated echoes of Quietist spirituality reappeared a few years later in France, in the work of the mystic Madame Guyon, whose doctrine of the disinterested «pure love» of God attracted Archbishop François Fénelon, tutor of the grandson of Louis XIV. The resulting controversy — dubbed «semi-Quietism» — set Fénelon against the powerful Bishop Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, already known to the reader of these pages for his defense of Gallicanism: the Conferences of Issy, in 1694, produced no satisfactory agreement, and Fénelon's book of defense, «Explanation of the Maxims of the Saints» (1697), was finally condemned by Pope Innocent XII in the brief «Cum Alias» (1699), which reprobated twenty-three propositions without, however, expressly qualifying them as heretical; Fénelon submitted immediately to the decision.

The episode of Quietism left as a lasting legacy a sharper dividing line, in Catholic spiritual theology, between the legitimate forms of passive and mystical contemplation — practiced and taught, for example, by Saint Teresa of Ávila and Saint John of the Cross — and formulations that, by radicalizing the passivity of the soul before God, risk emptying out moral responsibility and the active role of the human will in the Christian life.
itens.condenacao: Apostolic Constitution «Coelestis Pastor», of Innocent XI (1687)

itens.resumo: A period in which two, and later three, claimants simultaneously contested recognition by Western Christendom as the legitimate pope.
itens.corpo:
Between 1309 and 1377, seven successive popes had resided not in Rome but in Avignon, in southern France, under strong influence from the French crown — a period that the poet Petrarch would call the "Babylonian captivity" of the papacy. Pressed by the fervent appeals of mystics such as Catherine of Siena and Bridget of Sweden, Pope Gregory XI finally returned the papal see to Rome in January 1377, but he died the following year, in March 1378, reopening the question of the papal residence at a moment of acute instability.

Under heavy pressure from a Roman crowd that demanded an Italian pope — even surrounding the site of the conclave — the cardinals elected in April 1378 the Neapolitan archbishop Bartolomeo Prignano, who took the name Urban VI. The new pope proved, however, to be authoritarian and harsh in temperament, to the point of publicly humiliating several of the very cardinals who had elected him; already in August of the same year, most of them — mainly French — gathered at Fondi and declared the April election invalid, claiming that it had been held under duress from the Roman tumult, and elected in his place Robert of Geneva, a cousin of the king of France, who took the name Clement VII and settled in Avignon. Catherine of Siena, for her part, vigorously defended the legitimacy of Urban VI in fervent letters until her death in 1380.

Western Christendom thus found itself divided between two rival obediences, each recognizing a different pope according to the political alliances of the moment: France, the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon, Scotland and, for a time, Naples aligned themselves with Clement VII and his successors in Avignon, while the Holy Roman Empire, England, most of Italy, Portugal and Scandinavia recognized Urban VI and the Roman popes who succeeded him, Boniface IX, Innocent VII and Gregory XII. The rupture, purely jurisdictional and without any underlying doctrinal controversy, nonetheless split dioceses, religious orders and entire universities.

Successive attempts to negotiate the simultaneous resignation of the two popes (the so-called "via cessionis") failed, leading a group of cardinals from both obediences to convene, on their own initiative and without papal authorization, a council at Pisa in 1409. The assembly deposed both Gregory XII and the then Avignon pope, Benedict XIII, and elected a third claimant, Alexander V — but since neither of the deposed popes recognized the legitimacy of the council or actually stepped down, the practical result was, paradoxically, to worsen the crisis, with three simultaneous popes contesting recognition.

The definitive solution would come only from the Council of Constance (1414-1418), convened under strong pressure from Emperor Sigismund and bringing together the largest ecclesiastical assembly of the Middle Ages. In 1415 the council promulgated the decree "Haec Sancta," affirming that conciliar authority derives directly from Christ and that even the pope owes it obedience in matters of faith, the eradication of the schism and the reform of the Church — the doctrinal foundation of so-called conciliarism, whose exact relationship with the papal primacy would remain a subject of theological debate for centuries, until it was resolved in the opposite sense by the First Vatican Council in 1870. Under the authority thus claimed, the council deposed Pope John XXIII (successor of Alexander V, in the Pisan line) and the Avignon pope Benedict XIII, by then already a refugee in the castle of Peñíscola in Spain, where he would continue to claim the tiara until his death in 1423, never accepting his deposition; the Roman pope Gregory XII, for his part, avoided the precedent of being deposed by resigning voluntarily in 1415, thereby retroactively legitimizing the authority of the very council that he himself had formally reconvened.

Finally free of the three claimants, the Council of Constance unanimously elected, on November 11, 1417, the Roman cardinal Oddone Colonna, who took the name Martin V — a date that marks the end of almost four decades of institutional division in Latin Christendom. The same council, moved by the same spirit of reform that the Schism had exposed as urgent, also tried and had executed the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus in 1415 (see the corresponding entry). Unlike the Christological heresies of the first centuries, the Western Schism did not involve a declared doctrinal error, but a jurisdictional and disciplinary rupture over the legitimacy of the exercise of the Petrine primacy; the loss of credibility suffered by the papacy would feed, in the following decades, both the persistent strength of conciliarism and the general climate of criticism of the ecclesiastical institution that would prepare the ground, a century later, for the Protestant Reformation.
itens.condenacao: Council of Constance (1414-1418), which deposed the three claimants and elected Martin V
